claim: Cross-modal temporal recalibration guarantees stable temporal perception across ever-changing environments.
source: Cross-modal temporal recalibration guarantees stable temporal perception across ever-changing environments.
evidence: This is a general statement about the function of cross-modal temporal recalibration, presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The mechanisms of cross-modal temporal recalibration remain unknown.
source: Yet, the mechanisms of cross-modal temporal recalibration remain unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: Recalibration effects plateaued with increasing audiovisual asynchrony.
source: Consistent with previous findings, recalibration effects plateaued with increasing audiovisual asynchrony (nonlinearity) and varied by which modality led during the exposure phase (asymmetry).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data collected in this study and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: Recalibration effects varied by which modality led during the exposure phase.
source: Consistent with previous findings, recalibration effects plateaued with increasing audiovisual asynchrony (nonlinearity) and varied by which modality led during the exposure phase (asymmetry).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing asymmetry in recalibration effects.

claim: The causal-inference observer shifts the audiovisual temporal bias to compensate for perceived asynchrony, which is inferred by considering two causal scenarios: when the audiovisual stimuli have a common cause or separate causes.
source: The causal-inference observer shifts the audiovisual temporal bias to compensate for perceived asynchrony, which is inferred by considering two causal scenarios: when the audiovisual stimuli have a common cause or separate causes.
evidence: This describes the theoretical framework of the causal-inference model proposed in the study.

claim: The asynchrony-contingent observer updates the bias to achieve simultaneity of auditory and visual measurements, modulating the update rate by the likelihood of the audiovisual stimuli originating from a simultaneous event.
source: The asynchrony-contingent observer updates the bias to achieve simultaneity of auditory and visual measurements, modulating the update rate by the likelihood of the audiovisual stimuli originating from a simultaneous event.
evidence: This describes the theoretical framework of the asynchrony-contingent model.

claim: In the asynchrony-correction model, the observer first assesses whether the sensory measurement is asynchronous; if so, she adjusts the bias proportionally to the magnitude of the measured asynchrony.
source: In the asynchrony-correction model, the observer first assesses whether the sensory measurement is asynchronous; if so, she adjusts the bias proportionally to the magnitude of the measured asynchrony.
evidence: This describes the theoretical framework of the asynchrony-correction model.

claim: A Bayesian model comparison revealed that both the causal-inference process and modality-specific precision in arrival latency are required to capture the nonlinearity and asymmetry observed in audiovisual temporal recalibration.
source: A Bayesian model comparison revealed that both the causal-inference process and modality-specific precision in arrival latency are required to capture the nonlinearity and asymmetry observed in audiovisual temporal recalibration.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the model comparison analysis performed on the experimental data.

claim: Audiovisual temporal recalibration relies on the same causal-inference processes that govern cross-modal perception.
source: Our findings support the hypothesis that audiovisual temporal recalibration relies on the same causal-inference processes that govern cross-modal perception.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model comparison results.

claim: Misalignment across the senses can occur because signals in different modalities may arrive with different physical and neural delays in the relevant brain areas.
source: In a multimodal environment, misalignment across the senses can occur because signals in different modalities may arrive with different physical and neural delays in the relevant brain areas (Fain, 2019; Badde et al., 2020a; Pöppel, 1988; Spence and Squire, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Perceptual misalignment can arise from changes in the environment, such as when wearing a virtual-reality headset or adapting to hearing aids.
source: Perceptual misalignment can also arise from changes in the environment, such as when wearing a virtual-reality headset or adapting to hearing aids.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about how environmental changes affect perception.

claim: Cross-modal temporal recalibration serves as a critical mechanism to maintain perceptual synchrony despite changes in the perceptual systems and the environment.
source: Cross-modal temporal recalibration serves as a critical mechanism to maintain perceptual synchrony despite changes in the perceptual systems and the environment (reviewed in King, 2005; Vroomen and Keetels, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by review articles cited.

claim: Exposure to a consistent audiovisual stimulus-onset asynchrony (SOA) shifts the point of subjective simultaneity (PSS) between auditory and visual stimuli.
source: This phenomenon is exemplified in audiovisual temporal recalibration, where exposure to a consistent audiovisual stimulus-onset asynchrony (SOA) shifts the point of subjective simultaneity (PSS) between auditory and visual stimuli; as a result, stimuli at first perceived as temporally discrepant are gradually perceived as more synchronous (Di Luca et al., 2009; Fujisaki et al., 2004; Hanson et al., 2008; Harrar and Harris, 2008; Heron et al., 2007; Keetels and Vroomen, 2007; Navarra et al., 2005; Roach et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2011; Vatakis et al., 2007; Vatakis et al., 2008; Vroomen et al., 2004; Vroomen and Keetels, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Stimuli at first perceived as temporally discrepant are gradually perceived as more synchronous after exposure to consistent audiovisual SOA.
source: This phenomenon is exemplified in audiovisual temporal recalibration, where exposure to a consistent audiovisual stimulus-onset asynchrony (SOA) shifts the point of subjective simultaneity (PSS) between auditory and visual stimuli; as a result, stimuli at first perceived as temporally discrepant are gradually perceived as more synchronous (Di Luca et al., 2009; Fujisaki et al., 2004; Hanson et al., 2008; Harrar and Harris, 2008; Heron et al., 2007; Keetels and Vroomen, 2007; Navarra et al., 2005; Roach et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2011; Vatakis et al., 2007; Vatakis et al., 2008; Vroomen et al., 2004; Vroomen and Keetels, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Current models of audiovisual temporal recalibration either did not specify the recalibration process or did not capture all characteristics of recalibration effects.
source: However, the mechanisms of cross-modal temporal recalibration remain unknown. Current models of audiovisual temporal recalibration either did not specify the recalibration process (Di Luca et al., 2009 ; Navarra et al., 2009; Yarrow et al., 2015), or did not capture all characteristics of recalibration effects (Roach et al., 2011; Sato and Aihara, 2011; Yarrow et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous models.

claim: The amount of recalibration is not a linear function of the adapter SOA, but instead plateaus at an SOA of approximately 100–300 ms.
source: The amount of recalibration is not a linear function of the adapter SOA, but instead plateaus at an SOA of approximately 100–300 ms (Fujisaki et al., 2004; Vroomen et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recalibration magnitude differs depending on whether the visual or auditory stimulus leads during the exposure phase.
source: Recalibration can also be asymmetrical: its magnitude differs depending on whether the visual or auditory stimulus leads during the exposure phase (Fujisaki et al., 2004; O'Donohue et al., 2022; Van der Burg et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Causal inference is the process by which the observer determines whether multisensory signals originate from a common source and adjust their perceptual estimates accordingly.
source: Causal inference is the process by which the observer determines whether multisensory signals originate from a common source and adjust their perceptual estimates accordingly (Sato et al., 2007; Shams and Beierholm, 2010; Wei and Körding, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research defining causal inference.

claim: Bayesian models based on causal inference have been proposed to explain multisensory integration effects.
source: Bayesian models based on causal inference have been proposed to explain multisensory integration effects (Körding et al., 2007; Sato et al., 2007), and these models have been empirically validated in studies of spatial audiovisual and visual-tactile integration (Badde et al., 2020b; Beierholm et al., 2009; Rohe and Noppeney, 2015; Wozny et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Causal inference models have been empirically validated in studies of spatial audiovisual and visual-tactile integration.
source: Bayesian models based on causal inference have been proposed to explain multisensory integration effects (Körding et al., 2007; Sato et al., 2007), and these models have been empirically validated in studies of spatial audiovisual and visual-tactile integration (Badde et al., 2020b; Beierholm et al., 2009; Rohe and Noppeney, 2015; Wozny et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some studies have successfully used causal inference to model the integration of cross-modal relative timing, accurately predicting simultaneity judgments in audiovisual speech.
source: In the temporal domain, some studies have successfully used causal inference to model the integration of cross-modal relative timing, accurately predicting simultaneity judgments in audiovisual speech (Magnotti et al., 2013) and more complex scenarios involving one auditory and two visual stimuli (Sato, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Causal inference has been used to model more complex scenarios involving one auditory and two visual stimuli.
source: In the temporal domain, some studies have successfully used causal inference to model the integration of cross-modal relative timing, accurately predicting simultaneity judgments in audiovisual speech (Magnotti et al., 2013) and more complex scenarios involving one auditory and two visual stimuli (Sato, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The amount of recalibration should be reduced when the multisensory signals are not perceived as causally related.
source: In the context of cross-modal recalibration, causal inference is expected to play a role based on the intuition that the amount of recalibration should be reduced when the multisensory signals are not perceived as causally related (Fujisaki et al., 2004; Hsiao et al., 2022; Vroomen et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and represents an intuitive expectation.

claim: Causal-inference models successfully predicted cross-modal spatial recalibration of visual-auditory signals.
source: Supporting this, causal-inference models successfully predicted cross-modal spatial recalibration of visual-auditory (Hong, 2023; Hong et al., 2021; Sato et al., 2007) and visuo-tactile (Badde et al., 2020b) signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Causal-inference models successfully predicted cross-modal spatial recalibration of visuo-tactile signals.
source: Supporting this, causal-inference models successfully predicted cross-modal spatial recalibration of visual-auditory (Hong, 2023; Hong et al., 2021; Sato et al., 2007) and visuo-tactile (Badde et al., 2020b) signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The causal-inference model for cross-modal temporal recalibration derives the multisensory percept based on inferences about the shared origin of the signals and updates the cross-modal temporal biases such that subsequent measurements are shifted toward the percept.
source: Building on this framework, here, we propose a causal-inference model for cross-modal temporal recalibration that derives the multisensory percept based on inferences about the shared origin of the signals and updates the cross-modal temporal biases such that subsequent measurements are shifted toward the percept.
evidence: This describes the theoretical framework of the proposed causal-inference model.

claim: The asynchrony-contingent model predicts a nonlinear recalibration effect across adapter SOAs without requiring observers to perform full Bayesian inference.
source: The model predicts a nonlinear recalibration effect across adapter SOAs without requiring observers to perform full Bayesian inference.
evidence: This describes a prediction of the asynchrony-contingent model.

claim: The asynchrony-correction model predicts minimal recalibration when the adapter SOA falls within the range of measured asynchronies that can arise with simultaneously presented stimuli due to sensory noise.
source: Unlike the causal-inference and the asynchrony-contingent models, this model predicts minimal recalibration when the adapter SOA falls within the range of measured asynchronies that can arise with simultaneously presented stimuli due to sensory noise.
evidence: This describes a prediction of the asynchrony-correction model.

claim: The asymmetry may be explained by physical and neural latency differences between signals.
source: It has been suggested that the asymmetry may be explained by physical and neural latency differences between signals (O'Donohue et al., 2022; Van der Burg et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Latency differences can vary significantly based on the physical distance between the stimulus and the sensors, as well as the neural transmission time required for the signal to reach the relevant sensory region.
source: These latency differences can vary significantly based on the physical distance between the stimulus and the sensors, as well as the neural transmission time required for the signal to reach the relevant sensory region (Hirsh and Sherrick, 1961; King, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Latency differences vary with sensory experience in infancy.
source: Yet–speaking against a merely physical origin–these latency differences vary with sensory experience in infancy (Badde et al., 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Latency differences can explain the audiovisual temporal bias observed in most humans.
source: While these latency differences can explain the audiovisual temporal bias observed in most humans, they would affect recalibration to different adapter SOAs equally, making it unlikely for any asymmetry to arise.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of latency differences.

claim: Latency differences would affect recalibration to different adapter SOAs equally, making it unlikely for any asymmetry to arise.
source: While these latency differences can explain the audiovisual temporal bias observed in most humans, they would affect recalibration to different adapter SOAs equally, making it unlikely for any asymmetry to arise.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of latency differences.

claim: Sensory uncertainty has been shown to affect the degree of cross-modal recalibration in a complex fashion.
source: In contrast to latency differences, sensory uncertainty has been shown to affect the degree of cross-modal recalibration in a complex fashion (Badde et al., 2020b; Hong et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The difference across modalities in the precision of the arrival times plays a critical role in the asymmetry of cross-modal temporal recalibration.
source: We hypothesized that the difference across modalities in the precision of the arrival times, the time it takes visual and auditory signals to arrive in the relevant brain areas, plays a critical role in the asymmetry of cross-modal temporal recalibration.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Participants completed nine sessions on separate days.
source: In total, participants completed nine sessions on separate days.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The adapter SOA was fixed within each session, but varied randomly across sessions and in random order across participants.
source: The adapter SOA (range: –0.7 to 0.7 s) was fixed within each session, but varied randomly across sessions and in random order across participants.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: We observed an asymmetry in the amount of recalibration between auditory-leading and visual-leading adapter SOAs, with auditory-leading adapter SOAs inducing a greater amount of recalibration.
source: Additionally, we observed an asymmetry in the amount of recalibration between auditory-leading and visual-leading adapter SOAs, with auditory-leading adapter SOAs inducing a greater amount of recalibration (Figure 2B; see Appendix 2—figure 1A for individual participants' data).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the experimental data, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Eight out of nine participants showed an asymmetry index significantly different from zero.
source: Eight out of nine participants showed an asymmetry index significantly different from zero, with the majority showing greater recalibration for auditory-leading adapter SOAs, suggesting a general asymmetry in recalibration (Appendix 2—figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding based on statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The majority of participants showed greater recalibration for auditory-leading adapter SOAs.
source: Eight out of nine participants showed an asymmetry index significantly different from zero, with the majority showing greater recalibration for auditory-leading adapter SOAs, suggesting a general asymmetry in recalibration (Appendix 2—figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding based on the experimental data.

claim: Arrival times for the two modalities are independent.
source: We assume arrival times for the two modalities are independent and that the arrival latencies are exponentially distributed (García-Pérez and Alcalá-Quintana, 2012; Figure 3A, left panel).
evidence: This is an assumption of the model, with reference to previous work and Figure 3A.

claim: The arrival latencies are exponentially distributed.
source: We assume arrival times for the two modalities are independent and that the arrival latencies are exponentially distributed (García-Pérez and Alcalá-Quintana, 2012; Figure 3A, left panel).
evidence: This is an assumption of the model, with reference to previous work and Figure 3A.

claim: A constant offset exists between auditory and visual arrival times, reflecting an audiovisual temporal bias.
source: Moreover, we assume a constant offset between auditory and visual arrival times, reflecting an audiovisual temporal bias.
evidence: This is an assumption of the model.

claim: The resulting measurement of SOA has a double-exponential distribution.
source: A simple derivation shows that the resulting measurement of SOA has a double-exponential distribution (Figure 3A, right panel; see derivation in Appendix 3).
evidence: This is a mathematical derivation from the model assumptions, with reference to Figure 3A and Appendix 3.

claim: When the precision differs between modalities, the measurement distribution of the SOA between the auditory and visual stimuli is asymmetrical.
source: When the precision differs between modalities, the measurement distribution of the SOA between the auditory and visual stimuli is asymmetrical (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a consequence of the model assumptions, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Temporal recalibration is defined as the accumulation of updates to the audiovisual temporal bias after each encounter with an SOA.
source: Second, these models define temporal recalibration as the accumulation of updates to the audiovisual temporal bias after each encounter with an SOA.
evidence: This is a definition used in the models.

claim: The accumulated shift in the audiovisual bias at the end of the exposure phase is carried over to the post-test phase and persists throughout.
source: The accumulated shift in the audiovisual bias at the end of the exposure phase is then carried over to the post-test phase and persists throughout.
evidence: This is an assumption of the models.

claim: The bias is assumed to be reset to the same initial value in the pre-test across all nine sessions, reflecting the stability of the audiovisual temporal bias over time.
source: Lastly, the bias is assumed to be reset to the same initial value in the pre-test across all nine sessions, reflecting the stability of the audiovisual temporal bias over time (Grabot and van Wassenhove, 2017).
evidence: This is an assumption of the models, supported by a citation.

claim: The causal-inference model had the strongest model evidence at the group level and best fit the data of most participants.
source: To quantify model performance, we calculated model evidence, i.e., the likelihood of each model given the data marginalized over all possible parameters, which revealed that the causal-inference model had the strongest model evidence at the group level and best fit the data of most participants, followed by the asynchrony-contingent model and then the asynchrony-correction model.
evidence: This is a finding based on the model comparison analysis.

claim: Within each of the three model categories, the version incorporating modality-specific precision consistently outperformed the modality-independent version.
source: Within each of these three model categories, the version incorporating modality-specific precision consistently outperformed the modality-independent version.
evidence: This is a finding based on the model comparison analysis.

claim: The nonlinearity of audiovisual temporal recalibration across adapter SOAs was captured by both the asynchrony-contingent and causal-inference models.
source: The nonlinearity of audiovisual temporal recalibration across adapter SOAs was captured by both the asynchrony-contingent and causal-inference models.
evidence: This is a finding based on the model predictions compared to the data.

claim: The causal-inference model outperformed the asynchrony-contingent model by accurately predicting a non-zero average recalibration effect at adapter SOAs of 0.7 and –0.7 s.
source: Nonetheless, the causal-inference model outperformed the asynchrony-contingent model by accurately predicting a non-zero average recalibration effect at adapter SOAs of 0.7 and –0.7 s, where the asynchrony-contingent model predicted no recalibration.
evidence: This is a finding based on the model predictions compared to the data.

claim: Incorporating modality-specific precision enabled both the asynchrony-contingent and causal-inference models to more accurately predict increased recalibration when the adapter SOA was auditory-leading.
source: Additionally, incorporating modality-specific precision enabled both the asynchrony-contingent and causal-inference models to more accurately predict increased recalibration when the adapter SOA was auditory-leading.
evidence: This is a finding based on the model predictions compared to the data.

claim: The model that relies on causal inference during the exposure phase and assumes modality-specific precision of arrival times most accurately captured both the nonlinearity and asymmetry of the recalibration effect.
source: Overall, the model that relies on causal inference during the exposure phase and assumes modality-specific precision of arrival times most accurately captured both the nonlinearity and asymmetry of the recalibration effect.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model comparison and predictions.

claim: The prior belief that the auditory and visual stimuli share a common cause plays a crucial role in adjudicating the relative influence of the two causal scenarios.
source: The prior belief that the auditory and visual stimuli share a common cause plays a crucial role in adjudicating the relative influence of the two causal scenarios (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding based on model simulations, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: When the observer has a prior belief that audiovisual stimuli always originate from the same source, they recalibrate by a proportion of the perceived SOA no matter how large the measured SOA is.
source: When the observer has a prior belief that audiovisual stimuli always originate from the same source, they recalibrate by a proportion of the perceived SOA no matter how large the measured SOA is, mirroring the behavior of the asynchrony-correction model when its criteria for simultaneity are such that no stimuli are treated as simultaneous.
evidence: This is a finding based on model simulations.

claim: When the observer believes that the audiovisual stimuli always have separate causes, they treat the audiovisual stimuli as independent of each other and do not recalibrate.
source: On the other hand, when the observer believes that the audiovisual stimuli always have separate causes, they treat the audiovisual stimuli as independent of each other and do not recalibrate.
evidence: This is a finding based on model simulations.

claim: Non-zero recalibration effect for large adapter SOAs can be replicated by either assuming a strong prior for a common cause or by assuming low sensory precision of arrival times.
source: This non-zero recalibration effect for large adapter SOAs can be replicated by either assuming a strong prior for a common cause (Figure 5A) or by assuming low sensory precision of arrival times (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding based on model simulations, with reference to Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: Observers with a stronger prior belief in a common cause are more likely to assign a higher posterior probability to the common-cause scenario, leading to greater recalibration.
source: Both relationships are intuitive: observers with a stronger prior belief in a common cause and ideal observers with lower sensory precision are more likely to assign a higher posterior probability to the common-cause scenario, leading to greater recalibration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model simulations.

claim: Ideal observers with lower sensory precision are more likely to assign a higher posterior probability to the common-cause scenario, leading to greater recalibration.
source: Both relationships are intuitive: observers with a stronger prior belief in a common cause and ideal observers with lower sensory precision are more likely to assign a higher posterior probability to the common-cause scenario, leading to greater recalibration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model simulations.

claim: Differences in arrival-time precision between audition and vision result in an asymmetry of audiovisual temporal recalibration across adapter SOAs.
source: Differences in arrival-time precision between audition and vision result in an asymmetry of audiovisual temporal recalibration across adapter SOAs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding based on model simulations, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: The amount of recalibration is attenuated when the modality with the higher precision lags the less precise one during the exposure phase.
source: The amount of recalibration is attenuated when the modality with the higher precision lags the less precise one during the exposure phase.
evidence: This is a finding based on model simulations.

claim: When the more recent stimulus component in a cross-modal pair is more precise, the observer is more likely to attribute the asynchrony to separate causes and thus recalibrate less.
source: When the more recent stimulus component in a cross-modal pair is more precise, the observer is more likely to attribute the asynchrony to separate causes and thus recalibrate less.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model simulations.

claim: The fixed audiovisual bias does not affect asymmetry, but shifts the recalibration function laterally and determines the adapter SOA for which no recalibration occurs.
source: In addition, the fixed audiovisual bias does not affect asymmetry, but shifts the recalibration function laterally and determines the adapter SOA for which no recalibration occurs (Appendix 7—figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding based on model simulations, with reference to Appendix 7—figure 1B.

claim: Human observers rely on causal-inference-based percepts to recalibrate cross-modal temporal perception.
source: These findings suggest that human observers rely on causal-inference-based percepts to recalibrate cross-modal temporal perception.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model comparison results.

claim: The results align closely with studies that have demonstrated the role of causal inference in audiovisual and visual-tactile spatial recalibration.
source: These results align closely with studies that have demonstrated the role of causal inference in audiovisual (Hong et al., 2021) and visual-tactile spatial recalibration (Badde et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous research, supported by citations.

claim: The results are consistent with previous recalibration models that assumed a strong relation between perception and recalibration.
source: Our results are also consistent with previous recalibration models that assumed a strong relation between perception and recalibration (Sato and Aihara, 2011; Sato et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous research, supported by citations.

claim: The same mechanisms underlie cross-modal perception and recalibration across different sensory features.
source: Hence, we suggest that the same mechanisms underlie cross-modal perception and recalibration across different sensory features.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results and comparison to previous research.

claim: The asynchrony-contingent model failed to capture a non-zero recalibration effect at large adapter SOAs, as observed in several participants.
source: Even though this model was capable of predicting a nonlinear relationship between the recalibration effect and the adapter SOA, it failed to capture a non-zero recalibration effect at large adapter SOAs, as observed in several participants.
evidence: This is a finding based on comparing model predictions to the data.

claim: The asynchrony-contingent model uses the likelihood of a synchronous audiovisual stimulus pair given the measured SOA to modulate the update rate of audiovisual bias, which will be very small on average for large SOAs.
source: This is becausethis model uses the likelihood of a synchronous audiovisual stimulus pair given the measured SOA to modulate the update rate of audiovisual bias, which will be very small on average for large SOAs.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model's behavior based on its formulation.

claim: The causal-inference model can capture the non-zero recalibration effect because the common-cause scenario always influences the amount of recalibration even when the adapter SOA is too large to be perceived as synchronous.
source: In contrast, the causal-inference model can capture the non-zero recalibration effect because the common-cause scenario always influences the amount of recalibration even when the adapter SOA is too large to be perceived as synchronous.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model's behavior based on its formulation.

claim: A strong prior belief in a common cause or less precision of arrival times can result in non-zero recalibration effects following exposure to clearly asynchronous stimulus pairs.
source: Simulation (Figure 5A and B) shows that a strong prior belief in a common cause or less precision of arrival times can result in non-zero recalibration effects following exposure to clearly asynchronous stimulus pairs.
evidence: This is a finding based on model simulations, with reference to Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: Cross-modal temporal recalibration can be elicited by clearly asynchronous streams of sensory information.
source: Notably, even though it might at first seem counter-intuitive that cross-modal temporal recalibration can be elicited by clearly asynchronous streams of sensory information, many of us have experienced this effect during laggy, long video conferences.
evidence: This is an observation based on common experience.

claim: The asynchrony-correction model predicts recalibration effects across adapter SOAs that are contrary to our observations.
source: The asynchrony-correction model assumes that observers recalibrate to restore temporal synchrony whenever the SOA measurement indicates a temporal discrepancy, but this model predicts recalibration effects across adapter SOAs that are contrary to our observations.
evidence: This is a finding based on comparing model predictions to the data.

claim: Cross-modal temporal recalibration is not merely triggered by an asynchronous sensory measurement of SOA and an attempt to correct it.
source: This suggests that cross-modal temporal recalibration is not merely triggered by an asynchronous sensory measurement of SOA and an attempt to correct it.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model comparison results.

claim: The causal-inference model accurately captured the plateau of the recalibration effects as adapter SOA increased, because the probability that the auditory and visual stimuli have separate causes also increased.
source: In contrast, the causal-inference model accurately captured the plateau of the recalibration effects as adapter SOA increased, because the probability that the auditory and visual stimuli have separate causes also increased.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model's behavior based on its formulation and comparison to data.

claim: Most participants exhibited larger recalibration effects in response to exposure to audiovisual stimuli with a consistent auditory lead compared to exposure to a visual lead.
source: We found that most of our participants exhibited larger recalibration effects in response to exposure to audiovisual stimuli with a consistent auditory lead compared to exposure to a visual lead.
evidence: This is a finding based on the experimental data.

claim: This result is consistent with a previous study that reported greater cumulative recalibration in response to audiovisual stimuli with an auditory lead at the group level.
source: This result is consistent with a previous study that reported greater cumulative recalibration in response to audiovisual stimuli with an auditory lead at the group level (O'Donohue et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous research, supported by a citation.

claim: The asymmetry in recalibration effects might be due to higher precision of auditory compared to visual arrival latencies.
source: Our simulation results further suggested that this asymmetry in recalibration effects might be due to higher precision of auditory compared to visual arrival latencies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model simulations.

claim: A few participants showed the opposite pattern: stronger recalibration effects following exposure to visual-leading audiovisual stimuli.
source: A few participants showed the opposite pattern: stronger recalibration effects following exposure to visual-leading audiovisual stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding based on the experimental data.

claim: Causal-inference models often reveal substantial individual differences in sensory noise.
source: This is not surprising, as causal-inference models often reveal substantial individual differences in sensory noise (Hong et al., 2021; Magnotti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A recent EEG study provided neural correlates for individual sensory noise by identifying correlations between neural-latency noise and behavioral sensory noise measured from simultaneity-judgment tasks for audiovisual, visuo-tactile, and audio-tactile pairs.
source: A recent EEG study further provided neural correlates for individual sensory noise by identifying correlations between neural-latency noise and behavioral sensory noise measured from simultaneity-judgment tasks for audiovisual, visuo-tactile, and audio-tactile pairs (Yarrow et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The model explains how individual differences in precision of arrival latency could contribute to the asymmetry in cross-modal temporal recalibration observed in previous studies.
source: Therefore, our model explains how individual differences in precision of arrival latency could contribute to the asymmetry in cross-modal temporal recalibration observed in previous studies.

claim: Fujisaki et al., 2004, found a slightly larger recalibration in response to audiovisual stimuli with a visual lead compared to an auditory lead.
